title: Kilby, Noyce and the planar process
text:
CHAPTER 6. INTEGRATED CIRCUITS AND MICROPROCESSORS
SECTION 6.1. KILBY, NOYCE AND THE PLANAR PROCESS

By the late 1950s transistors had replaced tubes, but computers were still built from thousands of separate components soldered onto circuit boards and wired together by hand. Every connection was a cost and a potential failure, and as designs grew the wiring itself became the limit, a problem engineers called the "tyranny of numbers." The integrated circuit (IC) solved it by making transistors, resistors, capacitors and their interconnections together on a single piece of semiconductor. This section explains the two inventions usually credited, Jack Kilby's at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce's at Fairchild, and the manufacturing breakthrough that made Noyce's version practical: Jean Hoerni's planar process.

1. The tyranny of numbers

A computer of the late 1950s might contain tens of thousands of transistors and diodes and many more resistors and capacitors, with hundreds of thousands of soldered joints. Military systems, especially missiles and aircraft, needed electronics that were smaller, lighter and more reliable than could be achieved this way. Reliability falls quickly as part counts rise: if each of N joints independently fails with probability p over some period, the probability that all survive is

    (1 - p)^N, approximately exp(-N * p) for small p

With N = 100,000 and p = 10^-5, that is exp(-1), about 37 percent. Halving p only goes so far; reducing N radically is the real answer.

Several approaches were tried, including "micromodules" (small standardized component wafers stacked and wired together), thin-film circuits, and "molecular electronics." In 1952 the British radar engineer Geoffrey Dummer publicly proposed building electronic equipment as a solid block with no connecting wires, layers of insulating, conducting, rectifying and amplifying materials. He is sometimes called "the prophet of integrated circuits," though his group did not produce a working device. The German engineer Werner Jacobi at Siemens had filed a patent in 1949 for a semiconductor amplifier with several transistors on one substrate, and other proposals followed in the 1950s, but none led to production.

2. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments (1958)

Jack Kilby (1923-2005) joined Texas Instruments in Dallas in the summer of 1958. New employees did not yet have vacation time, so he was left working in the nearly empty laboratory during the company's collective summer holiday. He reasoned that if all components could be made of the same semiconductor material, they could be made in one piece:

  - transistors and diodes from p-n junctions;
  - resistors from the bulk resistance of the semiconductor;
  - capacitors from reverse-biased p-n junctions (their depletion capacitance, Section 5.1).

Using germanium, the material for which TI had suitable "mesa" transistor technology, he built a phase-shift oscillator on a single small slice. On September 12, 1958, he demonstrated it to TI management: when power was applied, an oscilloscope showed a continuous sine wave. This is generally recognized as the first working integrated circuit.

Kilby's device was not a manufacturable product. Its components were connected by tiny gold wires bonded by hand ("flying wires"), and the components were not electrically isolated from each other in a way that would scale. But it proved the concept. Kilby filed a patent application in February 1959. He received the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics "for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit" (shared with Zhores Alferov and Herbert Kroemer for heterostructure work). He also co-invented the handheld electronic calculator at TI in the late 1960s.

3. Fairchild and the planar process

Recall from Section 5.2 that in 1957 eight scientists left Shockley Semiconductor to found Fairchild Semiconductor (the "traitorous eight": Julius Blank, Victor Grinich, Jean Hoerni, Eugene Kleiner, Jay Last, Gordon Moore, Robert Noyce and Sheldon Roberts). Fairchild first made silicon mesa transistors, so called because each transistor stood on a raised plateau etched out of the wafer, with the junction edges exposed at the sides. Exposed junctions were easily contaminated, which made the devices unreliable.

Jean Hoerni (1924-1997), a Swiss-born physicist, devised the planar process in 1958-1959. His key idea built on the work of Mohamed Atalla at Bell Labs (Section 5.3), who had shown in 1957 that a layer of silicon dioxide grown on silicon passivates its surface and that oxide can block dopant diffusion (Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derick at Bell Labs had earlier found that oxide could mask diffusion). Hoerni's process:

  1. Grow a layer of silicon dioxide (SiO2) on the silicon wafer by heating it in oxygen or steam.
  2. Use photolithography to open windows in the oxide where you want to dope.
  3. Diffuse dopant atoms into the silicon through the windows. The oxide blocks diffusion elsewhere.
  4. Regrow oxide over the window, and repeat for the next region (for example, base diffusion, then emitter diffusion inside it).

The crucial difference from the mesa process: the p-n junctions reach the surface underneath the protective oxide, rather than being exposed at an etched edge. They remain sealed and clean. And the whole wafer stays flat, "planar," so further layers can be patterned on top. Planar transistors were far more reliable and became Fairchild's product. Hoerni received a patent on the planar process in 1962.

4. Noyce's monolithic integrated circuit (1959)

Robert Noyce (1927-1990), Fairchild's co-founder and director of research, saw that the planar process solved the remaining problems of integration:

  Interconnection. Because the wafer surface is flat and covered with insulating oxide, you can evaporate a thin film of metal (aluminum) over the whole surface, then pattern it by photolithography into wires. The metal touches the silicon only where you have etched contact holes through the oxide. All the wiring is made at once, in the same batch process as the devices, instead of by hand.

  Isolation. Components on the same chip must be electrically separate except where intentionally wired. Noyce proposed using reverse-biased p-n junctions to isolate regions. Kurt Lehovec of Sprague Electric independently patented p-n junction isolation in 1959, and later historians, including Gordon Moore, have discussed how to credit him.

Noyce wrote up his concept in January 1959 and filed a patent in July 1959. On September 27, 1960, a group at Fairchild led by Jay Last produced the first operational planar integrated circuit, using Noyce's and Hoerni's ideas. In 1961 Fairchild introduced the Micrologic family of RTL logic ICs, among the first commercial ICs (Section 5.3), and Texas Instruments introduced its own IC line the same year.

Kilby's and Noyce's patents were the subject of a long legal battle between Texas Instruments and Fairchild. The companies eventually agreed to cross-license, and the industry convention has been to credit both men as co-inventors: Kilby for the first demonstration of an integrated circuit, Noyce for the practical monolithic silicon IC with integrated interconnections made by the planar process. Historians also emphasize that the group of essential contributors was larger, including Hoerni, Last, Lehovec and Atalla.

5. How a planar IC is made: photolithography

Photolithography is the technique that has scaled from features of tens of micrometers in 1960 to a few nanometers today. Its basic steps are still recognizably the same:

  1. Coat the oxidized wafer with photoresist, a light-sensitive polymer.
  2. Expose it to ultraviolet light through a mask (a glass plate with an opaque pattern), or, in modern systems, project a reduced image of the mask with a lens.
  3. Develop: the exposed resist (for positive resist) dissolves, leaving a resist pattern.
  4. Etch the oxide where it is not protected by resist (originally with hydrofluoric acid, now often with plasma).
  5. Strip the remaining resist.
  6. Process the exposed silicon: diffuse or implant dopants, deposit metal, and so on.
  7. Repeat with the next mask, carefully aligned to the previous layers.

An early IC needed perhaps four to six masks; a modern logic chip needs dozens of patterning steps and more than a dozen layers of metal interconnect. Ion implantation, which shoots dopant ions into the silicon at controlled energies, replaced diffusion from the 1970s onward for precise doping control.

The economics are what matter most. Everything on the wafer is made simultaneously, and many identical chips ("dies") are made on each wafer. The cost of a processed wafer depends only weakly on how many transistors are on it. So if you can shrink features, you get more transistors per chip and more chips per wafer at nearly the same cost. This is the economic engine behind Moore's law (Section 6.2).

Resolution. The smallest printable feature is roughly

    feature size is approximately k1 * lambda / NA

where lambda is the wavelength of the light, NA the numerical aperture of the projection lens, and k1 a process factor (with tricks, below about 0.3). The industry moved from mercury lamp lines (436 nm, 365 nm) to excimer lasers (248 nm, 193 nm) and, from around 2019 in high-volume production, to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light at 13.5 nm. EUV machines are made by a single company, ASML in the Netherlands, and these machines are among the most complex machines ever built. They are a strategic bottleneck in the production of the advanced chips used for AI.

Yield. Defects such as dust particles kill chips. A simple model (Poisson) gives yield

    Y = exp(-D * A)

where D is defect density per unit area and A is chip area. Bigger chips have exponentially lower yield. This is why cleanrooms are so clean, and why very large AI accelerator chips are engineering feats (some designs now combine several smaller "chiplets" in one package to manage yield).

6. Early ICs and the space and defense markets

Early ICs were expensive and used mostly where size, weight and reliability justified the cost. The US Air Force's Minuteman II missile guidance system and NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer were among the largest early customers. Apollo's purchase of Fairchild RTL NOR gates (Section 5.3) is often cited as having helped drive volume up and prices down in the early 1960s. By the late 1960s ICs were common in commercial computers and the "third generation" of computers, built from ICs, was established.

Integration levels grew through what were called:

    SSI  (small-scale integration):   up to about 10 gates per chip, early 1960s
    MSI  (medium-scale):              tens to hundreds of gates, late 1960s
    LSI  (large-scale):               thousands of gates, 1970s, the first microprocessors
    VLSI (very large-scale):          tens of thousands and more, from the late 1970s

Today a single AI accelerator chip contains tens of billions of transistors, and the term VLSI is used for all of it.

7. Why this matters for AI

The IC is the foundation of the scaling that made modern AI possible. Neural networks require huge numbers of multiply-accumulate operations and huge amounts of memory bandwidth. Only by integrating billions of transistors on a chip, wiring them with nanometer-scale metal, and making them by the million with photolithography, can hardware supply the roughly 10^15 or more operations per second that a modern accelerator delivers. The chain from Hoerni's oxide windows to an AI data center is unbroken.

8. Summary

  - Discrete-component electronics faced a "tyranny of numbers": reliability and cost limited the number of parts and connections.
  - Dummer (1952) and Jacobi (1949 patent) proposed integration; Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated the first working IC, a germanium oscillator, on September 12, 1958 (Nobel Prize, 2000).
  - Jean Hoerni's planar process at Fairchild (1958-1959) used silicon dioxide masks and passivation, based on Atalla's surface passivation work, to make flat, reliable devices.
  - Robert Noyce (patent filed July 1959) added integrated aluminum interconnections over the oxide and junction isolation (also patented by Lehovec); Jay Last's group made the first planar IC work on September 27, 1960.
  - Photolithography makes every transistor and wire on a wafer at once; feature size goes as k1 * lambda / NA, and yield falls with chip area, Y = exp(-D A).
  - Early ICs went to missiles and Apollo; integration progressed from SSI to VLSI and today's billions of transistors per chip.
